definition: Inundate means to flood or overwhelm with a huge amount.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inundate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inundate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The spring melt inundated the low pastures, and the ewes spent a week grazing the hill.
To dampen is the lightest touch of water — it stops a long way short of inundate, which buries a thing under it.
To soak drenches something through, yet still stops short of inundate, which covers and overwhelms it entirely.

To swamp is to bury something under more than it can handle -- the informal twin of inundate, at home in speech and email. Inundate does the same work in formal writing, and keeps the literal flood sense alive. Your inbox gets swamped; a report says the office was inundated.

A deluge pours down in torrents -- the word is more dramatic than inundate, painting the volume as a biblical downpour, water or mail alike. Inundate is the standard, neutral term for volume beyond capacity. Use deluge when you want the flood to sound spectacular.

To engulf is to swallow whole -- the thing disappears inside what covers it, a boat inside a wave, a house inside flames. Inundate overwhelms a thing's capacity while it struggles on above the flood. If the victim has vanished entirely, engulf is the word.

Inundate means to flood or overwhelm with a huge amount.
When the registrar posted the wrong grade cutoff, appeals inundated her office within a day — a stack by nine, a second clerk by noon, a locked door by Friday.
Inundate began as water — unda is Latin for 'wave' — and still does that literal work, but its daily job is volume that overwhelms capacity: appeals, complaints, entries.
Swamp and deluge are its close kin; sprinkle-scale words like dampen never qualify.
Inundate is the standard word for volume beyond capacity, literal floodwater or five hundred emails.
Swamp says the same thing informally; deluge is more dramatic.
If the amount is merely large but manageable, you were busy, not inundated.

The Harborview Fishing Museum had asked, in one modest online post, whether anyone still owned photographs of the old cannery row.
The post traveled further than its author dreamed.
By Friday the museum's single mail slot had jammed, and parcels were stacked against the door.
Within two weeks, donations inundated the little archive: four thousand photographs, nine hundred letters, and one improbable ship's bell.
The curator hired two students, bought a second scanner, and kept accepting.
'We are behind,' she wrote cheerfully, 'but we are open.' By spring the backlog had a filing system, and the cannery exhibit had tripled in size.
